idea.why: Genuinely multi-agent rather than one prompt wearing three hats, with the synthesiser explicitly told its job is only synthesis and never to repeat the specialists' lists. Each agent owns one source, one schema and one model, and nothing is split arbitrarily.

structure.why: Idiomatic node choices throughout. The Merge is the weak spot: it declares a data join with clash handling, but every downstream consumer reads through node references, so it is really a synchronisation barrier dressed as a merge.

connections.why: The wiring matches the real dependency graph exactly: fan-out to two independent fetches, each branch chained where dependent, rejoining at Merge inputs before the synthesiser, which genuinely needs both. Sub-node attachments are on the right ports and the tail is correctly serial.

answer.why: A reader would recognise this immediately, with empty-data paths handled rather than assumed. The honest gap is that the dashboard arrives only as an email with no served page, and the noise bucket is counted but never inspectable.

appraisal: The shape the brief actually asks for: two independent read-only specialists fanned out from one trigger, a synthesiser forbidden from repeating their work, and a purpose-built node rendering the result. The node vocabulary is right, with Aggregate instead of Code, structured parsers keeping each contract stable, and a cheaper model for sorting with a stronger one for narrative. The Merge is the least honest node: it declares a deep merge but both downstream nodes ignore the merged payload and reach back by reference, so it only gates timing. That reliance on paired-item resolution across a combine-all merge is the first thing to change, since lineage through a merge is exactly where these expressions break on real data.
